title: Some Perspective | The guided walkthrough

slides.title: India grew. Did that growth buy what it was supposed to?
slides.body: Between 2014 and 2026 India became the world's most populous country and the sixth-largest economy at market exchange rates (IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2026). Over the same years, every available measure of democratic quality fell. This walkthrough sets out what the data shows about whether those two facts were a trade, and concludes that they were not.
slides.note: Use the arrow keys, or swipe. Every figure here is read live from the site's dataset.

slides.title: The claimed bargain trades constraint for prosperity
slides.body: The strongest case for the period runs like this. A decisive executive, unencumbered by coalition bargaining, judicial review and federal veto points, can do things a constrained one cannot. Institutional constraint is the price, and material progress is what it buys.
points: That is a serious argument, and this project tests it.
A bargain requires both halves to be measured: what was given up, and what was received.
Most accounts measure only one half.

slides.title: The instruments needed to check also degraded
slides.body: Assessing performance after 2014 runs into a specific difficulty. The statistical apparatus that would register the answer was itself weakened during the period.
points: The 2021 census was postponed in 2020 with no new date. Houselisting began in April 2026 and population enumeration is notified for February 2027.
The 2017-18 consumption survey was completed, then withheld after it showed rural consumption falling.

The national accounts moved to a 2011-12 base in 2015, which raised measured growth for the years it covered. In 2018 a back-series drafted by a National Statistical Commission committee, which raised UPA-era growth, was shelved, and the back-series the CSO and NITI Aayog released instead lowered it. Neither revision was independently reviewed.
The two remaining non-official members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in January 2019, and the NSSO and the CSO were merged into the NSO.
Official COVID mortality was ~0.5 million against independent excess-mortality estimates of 3-5 million.
slides.note: Each is individually documented. The pattern matters because the withheld numbers were, with high consistency, the unfavourable ones.

slides.title: Three indices, one script, both eras
slides.body: To compare the UPA decade (2004-2013) with the NDA period (2014-2026) fairly, both are measured by the same instrument, a single deterministic script applied across the whole period. Any difference comes from the inputs, and none from the method.
points: SSI: Statistical Suppression Index, 0-10. Interference with official statistics.
FCI: Fiscal Centralisation Index, 0-1. Fiscal authority shifting from states to the union.
DQI: Democratic Quality Index, 0-1. Four published third-party democracy measures combined.

slides.title: Suppression rose and democratic quality fell after 2014
slides.body: SSI is zero across the entire UPA decade, peaks at {{max:economic.ssi}} in 2021-22, and is {{last:economic.ssi}} in 2026. DQI falls from {{first:eraHistory.dqi}} to {{last:economic.dqi}}; the 2026 value uses the latest published V-Dem and Freedom House scores, which cover 2025. FCI averages {{avg:eraHistory.fci}} under UPA and {{avg:economic.fci}} under NDA, peaks at {{max:economic.fci}} in 2020 and is {{last:economic.fci}} in 2026. Most of its NDA-era rise comes from GST and the 2020 borrowing conditions.
slides.note: The shaded band marks the NDA period. SSI is shown on its own 0-10 scale.
slides.chartAlt: Line chart, 2004 to 2026. The Statistical Suppression Index, the Fiscal Centralisation Index and the Democratic Quality Index, all rescaled to 0-10. The SSI rises after 2014 and peaks in 2021-22, the FCI peaks in 2020 and then falls, and the DQI falls from 0.49 in 2014 to 0.28 in 2026, with small rises in 2021 and 2025.

slides.title: From zero to nine, and it has not returned to zero
slides.body: The SSI weights six documented streams by how much each damages the public's ability to evaluate the government. The census delay carries the most weight, followed by the mortality undercount, the withheld consumption survey, the disputed GDP revision, the loss of institutional independence, and the employment-data delay.
points: No qualifying event occurred in 2004-2013, so that decade scores zero.
The 2021-22 peak of {{max:economic.ssi}} comes from these streams stacking up over several years.
It is {{last:economic.ssi}} in 2026. The census now has a schedule and counts as a delay, while the NSO merger and the shelved GDP back-series still count at full weight.

slides.kicker: The first half of the bargain
slides.title: Growth was about the same in both periods
slides.body: Real GDP growth averaged {{avg:eraHistory.gdpGrowth}}% across 2004-05 to 2013-14 and {{avg:economic.gdpGrowth}}% across 2014-15 to 2025-26. There is no annual estimate for 2026-27 yet.
points: The later figure includes the 2020-21 pandemic contraction of 5.8%, which accounts for all of the gap. Without that year the NDA average is 7.29%, above the UPA figure.
The earlier figure includes the 2008-09 global financial crisis year. Without it the UPA average is 7.23%, so with both shock years set aside the two periods grew at almost the same rate.
The two periods are also not cleanly comparable. The UPA years rest on a back-series whose method was disputed, and the years from 2023-24 sit on a new 2022-23 base released in February 2026.
Taking the official numbers at face value, growth did not accelerate after 2014.

slides.title: Formal job coverage fell while GDP grew
slides.body: On the Periodic Labour Force Survey, the share of all workers in regular wage or salaried jobs with any social security was {{first:economic.formalEmployment}}% in 2017-18. It fell to a low of {{min:economic.formalEmployment}}% in 2022-23 and was {{last:economic.formalEmployment}}% in 2023-24, while GDP grew in every year of that period except the pandemic year. Roughly nine in ten Indian workers have no social-security cover.
slides.note: Among regular wage and salaried employees, the share with no social security rose from 49.6% in 2017-18 to 53.4% in 2023-24. The survey begins in 2017-18, so it cannot show the years before it. The finding does not depend on the disputed national accounts.
slides.chartAlt: Combination chart. Bars show annual GDP growth from 2004 to 2026 against the left axis. A line shows formal employment as a percentage of all workers against the right axis, for the PLFS years 2017-18 to 2023-24 only. The line falls from 11.5% in 2017-18 to 9.6% in 2022-23, with a rise in 2021-22, and is 10.1% in 2023-24.

slides.title: The growth happened where the jobs are not
slides.body: Agriculture holds 43% of employment (PLFS, 2025) while producing about 18% of output. Manufacturing, the sector that in the standard development sequence absorbs that labour, holds only 12% of jobs.
slides.note: Industrial policy weighted toward capital-intensive sectors can raise output more than it raises employment.
slides.chartAlt: Grouped bar chart by sector, comparing each sector’s share of output with its share of jobs. The sectors holding most of the jobs hold much less of the output.

slides.title: The top 1% gained and the bottom half lost ground
slides.body: The top 1% income share rose from {{first:eraHistory.top1Share}}% in 2004 to {{last:economic.top1Share}}% in 2022-23. The bottom 50% share fell from {{first:eraHistory.bottom50Share}}% in 2004 to a low of {{min:economic.bottom50Share}}% in 2017 and was {{last:economic.bottom50Share}}% in 2022-23.
slides.note: At {{last:economic.top1Share}}%, the top 1% share is the highest in a series that begins in 1922, higher than in the inter-war colonial period (World Inequality Lab). The bottom 50% share rose a little in 2018-2020, which its authors describe as temporary. No annual figure is published for 2023 to 2026.
slides.chartAlt: Line chart of income shares from 2004 to 2022, the last published year. The top 1 per cent share rises. The bottom 50 per cent share falls to 2017 and then partly recovers.

slides.title: The one exception, and why it does not count as a win
slides.body: Consumer price inflation averaged {{avg:eraHistory.cpiInflation}}% in 2004-2013 against {{avg:economic.cpiInflation}}% in 2014-2026. It is the only measure moving the other way, and most of the movement has little to do with Indian policy.
points: The comparison straddles a global commodity cycle. Brent crude fell from about $115 a barrel in mid-2014 to under $30 by early 2016, driven by US shale supply and OPEC defending market share. India imported 88.2% of its crude oil in 2024-25 (PPAC, provisional).
An external shock that size, landing exactly at the boundary between the two periods, explains more of the gap than any change of government does.
Where domestic policy did help, it was inflation targeting, a rule that binds the executive's hands. That is a delegation of power away from the executive.
The 2026 figure also sits on a new CPI basket where food's weight fell from 45.9% to 36.8%, so it prints lower for the same price movements.
slides.note: The full argument, with six factors, the strongest case against us, and what would change our reading, is at someperspective.info/inflation.

slides.title: GDP counts the rent and leaves out the cooking
slides.body: Every growth figure in this deck is a GDP figure. GDP counts work inside a boundary somebody drew. Own the flat you live in and the accounts work out a rent you never paid and add it to output. Cook the evening meal in that flat and nothing is added.
points: India already counts the hours. The Time Use Survey found that women aged 6 and above who do unpaid domestic work spent 289 minutes a day on it in 2024 (305 minutes for women aged 15-59). Men spent 88.
At 289 minutes that is about 1,758 hours a year for a woman, in no employment figure and no output series.

Two survey rounds, five years apart, show little change in who does this work. The share of men doing any unpaid domestic work rose from 26.1% to 27.1%, against 81.2% and 81.5% for women. The minutes fell for both sexes, so the gap between a woman who does it and a man who does it went from 202 minutes to 201, a change of one minute in five years.

Published estimates of what the work is worth run from 7.5% to 32.4% of GDP, and one reported estimate reaches 36%. That spread is a disagreement about the price of an hour. There is little doubt about the hours.

It changes how to read one of our own numbers. About 40% of women aged 15 and over are counted in the labour force (PLFS, 2025), and the rest are often described as not working. The Time Use Survey found 81.5% of women aged 6 and above doing unpaid domestic work on the day it asked about in 2024.
slides.note: Nothing in this deck is adjusted for any of it. These are the official figures on the official boundary. The full argument is at someperspective.info/care.

slides.title: Eight of nine measures are worse, and one is better
slides.body: Comparing period averages across every directly comparable measure, the later period performs worse on eight and better on one.
slides.note: If the later period's statistics are biased in the government's favour, as the SSI argues, then this comparison understates the deterioration.
slides.chartAlt: Dumbbell chart of nine measures. For each, one marker is the UPA 2004-13 average and the other the NDA 2014-26 average, both placed within that measure’s own 2004-2026 range. Eight markers move towards the worse end.

slides.title: A decline comparable to Turkey's, from a higher base
slides.body: India's V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index fell from 0.488 in 2014 to 0.260 in 2025, a fall of 0.228 points. Turkey fell from 0.252 to 0.110, and Hungary from 0.521 to 0.315. Turkey's proportional fall is steeper, from a base already near the floor. India's is the largest absolute fall of the three.
slides.note: 2025 is V-Dem's latest observation (v16, March 2026). Brazil and South Africa, large democracies under real political stress over the same years, moved comparatively little. Whatever is happening in the measure globally, it is not marking every country down.
slides.chartAlt: Grouped bar chart comparing V-Dem liberal democracy scores in 2014 and 2025 for India and its peer countries.

slides.title: A different method reaches the same conclusion
slides.body: Kevin and Robin Grier (Texas Tech) build a synthetic counterfactual, a weighted blend of comparator countries fitted to India's path over 1984-2013, and measure the gap that opens after 2014. All ten governance indicators they test deteriorate, and the authors report a p-value of 0.00 for each.
slides.note: The method, the data and the authors are all different, and there is no shared machinery with this project. Their electoral-democracy gap in the final year is 0.391 points below the synthetic counterfactual, equal to 60.2% of India's 2013 score. India's own V-Dem Electoral Democracy Index fell from 0.617 in 2014 to 0.377 in 2025, a decline of 38.9%. The two measure different things, so the numbers are not directly comparable.
slides.chartAlt: Horizontal bar chart. For each indicator, the gap between India and its synthetic counterfactual, expressed as a percentage of India's 2013 level.

slides.title: The limits, stated plainly
slides.body: This project is descriptive. It establishes what happened on both dimensions. It does not identify a causal effect of governance on growth.
points: The author is a former Manmohan Singh Fellow of the All India Professionals' Congress, a department of the Indian National Congress, and this comparison runs in that party's favour. The work began before the fellowship. The interest is declared in full on the site. What is offered against it is that every input, every weighting and every step is published and can be recomputed.
The SSI's zero for the UPA decade is the most contestable number here, though the conclusion survives even a generous re-coding of that era.
The DQI inherits whatever biases exist in V-Dem, Freedom House and RSF.
The FCI is relative to its own sample and means nothing outside it.
The three indices are not independent evidence of one another. They plausibly measure one underlying process.
The window contains a pandemic, which supplies a legitimate reason for some of what the indices register.
slides.note: An error in this project's own documents, one that ran in its favour, was found and corrected in August 2026. It is reported in the paper.

slides.title: Statistical independence is the first reform
slides.body: Every other question (whether growth accelerated, whether poverty fell, whether welfare reached anyone) can only be settled against evidence produced by institutions willing to publish unfavourable findings.
points: Conduct the census. Publish consumption surveys on a fixed cycle regardless of what they show.
Restore the separation between the statistical office and the ministry it evaluates.
Refer the disputed GDP back-series to independent review.
After that come formalisation of employment, an industrial policy weighted toward labour absorption, and an explicit settlement on fiscal federalism.
slides.note: A government that did everything else on this list while leaving the statistical system alone would leave the public unable to tell whether any of it worked.

slides.title: All of this is open, and checkable
slides.body: Every figure in this walkthrough is read live from the same dataset the site and the paper use. Nothing here is a screenshot.
